subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that ∫₀^(π/2) x/(sinx + cosx) dx = π/(2√2) log(√2 + 1).

mark_split.label: Apply the property with a = π/2
Add to reach an x-free integral
Write cosx + sinx as √2 sin(x + π/4)

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book printed p.41 (PDF page 40) — LAQ chapter 4 'Definite Integrals', answer 35, the book's own 'BABY TIP' box on this page calls it 'VERY SIMILAR TO PREVIOUS SOLUTION' (answer 34, one page earlier). Printed appearance: TS 17, AP 20. Chapter star rank ★★★ applies. No margin mark tags are printed on this single-column page, so the 2+2+2+1 split is OURS, matching the split used for answer 34's near-identical derivation (ts_ipe_m2b_di_laq_sin2x_over_cosx_plus_sinx) and patterned on book p.22 answer 9's printed 2+2+2+1 shape. insider_note: The sub-integral ∫₀^(π/2) dx/(sinx+cosx) that appears here is the same helper integral as the preceding question (sin²x/(cosx+sinx)) — a student who reaches it should recognise the shortcut instead of re-deriving it from scratch.

steps.label: Apply the property with a = π/2
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Only the x in front changes — the denominator is unchanged, just like the previous question.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π/2 − x) + cos(π/2 − x) = cosx + sinx = sinx + cosx — the denominator is symmetric, so it never changes under this property.
lines: By x → π/2 − x: I = ∫₀^(π/2) (π/2 − x)/(sin(π/2 − x) + cos(π/2 − x)) dx
steps.why: The denominator sinx + cosx is symmetric under the swap sinx ↔ cosx, so it is unchanged by x → π/2 − x; only the numerator's x becomes π/2 − x, which is what makes the addition step work.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to change x to π/2 − x in the numerator as well as inside sin and cos.
Writing sin(π/2 − x) + cos(π/2 − x) as sinx − cosx instead of cosx + sinx.

steps.label: Add to reach an x-free integral
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. x + (π/2 − x) = π/2 is what cancels the x term.
steps.memory_tip: x + (π/2 − x) always cancels to a plain π/2 — the same cancellation trick used throughout this chapter.
steps.why: Adding the two equal forms cancels x and (π/2 − x) down to a plain π/2, leaving the same x-free integral that the preceding question also needed.
common_mistakes: Adding the numerators incorrectly and not getting the constant π/2.
Losing the factor of 1/2 when isolating I from 2I.

steps.label: Write cosx + sinx as √2 sin(x + π/4)
steps.margin_note: Two marks for the R sin(x+α) rewrite and the cosecant integral — identical setup to the previous question.
steps.memory_tip: sinx + cosx = √2 sin(x + π/4) — the same rewrite as the previous question, reused here.
lines: I = (π/(4√2))∫₀^(π/2) cosec(x + π/4) dx    [∵ ∫cosecθ dθ = log tan(θ/2)]
steps.why: The same R sin(x+α) rewrite used in the previous question reduces this integral to the identical cosecant form, only now multiplied by the extra factor of π/2 that came from the numerator.
common_mistakes: Missing the extra π/4 factor that appears here but not in the previous question.
Forgetting the 1/√2 factors inside the sine sum.

steps.label: Evaluate the log limits
steps.margin_note: The last mark. This is exactly the answer the question asks to show — underline it.
steps.memory_tip: tan(3π/8) = √2 + 1 and tan(π/8) = √2 − 1 — the same pair used in the previous question.
steps.why: Rationalising the fraction inside the log gives a perfect square, and log(a²) = 2 log(a) cancels the outer factor of 2 with the 4 in the denominator, leaving exactly the result the question asks to show.
common_mistakes: Not rationalising (√2+1)/(√2−1) before taking the log.
Arriving at a value that is off from the printed result by a factor of 2 — a sign that the log(a²) = 2log(a) step was skipped.
